methodology.context_policy: Each response turn is assessed against up to 3 immediately preceding chronological turns; target may be any different speaker in that window.
methodology.moderator_policy: Moderation, introductions, summaries, follow-up questions, and repetition without a stance are uncertain; substantive stances are classified normally. Host identity is not used for classification.
methodology.overlap_policy: Overlap and interruption are not evidence of stance by themselves.
methodology.uncertain_policy: Every eligible response turn receives one record; unclear or non-stance turns are classified uncertain.
methodology.target_policy: Target is a specific earlier turn; no reverse inference. Response timestamp determines subtopic mapping.

Rajdeep, this is a regime change operation and regime change in a democracy is called a no confidence motion. Their allies will lose confidence in them. Members of the Bharatiya Janata Party will lose confidence in them. This is a moral battle fought on Mahatma Gandhi's principles. Even the oppressor will realise that their oppression is no longer valid and that's why we will hit the streets. They will detain one, they will detain another.

I've listened to you, Anish, and I've listened to you, Sanju Verma. Thank you very much, Sanju Verma and Anish Gawande for joining me on the show. No, Madam, I have some time, seconds for my take on this special. State versus the street. It's been a turbulent week in Indian politics, with the battle moving from Parliament and television studios to the streets of this country. But here's a fundamental democratic principle. Protest is not a threat to democracy. It is a safety valve that keeps democracy alive. The state has every right, indeed a duty, to maintain law and order. But there is a crucial distinction between preventing violence and criminalizing dissent. or picking up someone from their house or an aircraft when they have not committed any crime. Peaceful protest is a constitutional right, not a favour granted by the government. When the state begins to see every gathering as a law and order problem, it risks turning a legitimate democratic demand into a confrontation. The state must maintain order, but not at the cost of liberty. A democracy should fear violence, not peaceful dissent. And yes, whether there is a regime change or not, will not be decided in the end with street protests. It will be decided by the ballot box. Let's leave it in the end to Janata Janardhan.
